yaml:
id: no-public-mutable-collection-val
language: kotlin
severity: warning
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: variable_declaration
        has:
          kind: user_type
          has:
            kind: type_identifier
            regex: '^(MutableList|MutableMap|MutableSet|MutableCollection|ArrayList|HashMap|LinkedHashMap|HashSet|LinkedHashSet)$'
    - not:
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'
          stopBy: end
    - inside:
        kind: class_body
    - not:
        inside:
          kind: class_declaration
          stopBy: end
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: visibility_modifier
              regex: '^(private|internal)$'
note: >-
  Public property exposes a mutable collection (MutableList/MutableMap/...).
  Callers can mutate it behind your back. Expose the read-only interface
  (List/Map/Set) via a public getter backed by a private mutable field.

id: no-var-in-object-declaration
language: kotlin
severity: error
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: binding_pattern_kind
        regex: '^var$'
    - inside:
        kind: class_body
        inside:
          kind: object_declaration
note: >-
  Mutable `var` inside a top-level/named `object` is process-wide shared
  mutable singleton state — a data race and a hidden global. Model state
  with a StateFlow/Mutex-guarded holder or pass it explicitly, not via a
  mutable singleton field.

id: no-volatile-var
language: kotlin
severity: warning
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: binding_pattern_kind
        regex: '^var$'
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has:
          kind: annotation
          has:
            kind: user_type
            has:
              kind: type_identifier
              regex: '^Volatile$'
note: >-
  @Volatile var is hand-rolled cross-thread shared mutable state. Prefer a
  StateFlow (for observable state) or a Mutex-guarded holder (for
  invariants) so reads/writes compose and stay race-free. If @Volatile is
  genuinely the right primitive, keep it private and document why.
badExample:
@Volatile
private var currentJob: Job? = null
goodExample:
private val _currentJob = MutableStateFlow<Job?>(null)
val currentJob: StateFlow<Job?> = _currentJob.asStateFlow()

id: no-loop-in-init
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: Imperative loop inside an init block. Move this construction logic into a factory function or compute it from typed members.
note: |
  An init block with a for/while loop that reassigns a `var` is non-trivial
  construction logic (here: building a middleware/decorator chain by mutating a
  `var` in a loop). It is hard to test in isolation and hides construction behind
  object creation. Prefer a private/companion factory function that returns the
  built value, then assign it: `val chain = buildChain(inner, middlewares)`.
  Tenet: explicit construction over magic; clean composable testable units.
  (require()/check() validation init blocks — including per-element validation
  loops that only call require/check — do NOT match this rule and are encouraged.)
rule:
  kind: anonymous_initializer
  has:
    stopBy: end
    any:
      - kind: for_statement
      - kind: while_statement
      - kind: do_while_statement
    has:
      stopBy: end
      kind: assignment

id: no-callback-wiring-in-init
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: Registering a lambda on a collaborator inside init leaks `this` before construction completes.
note: |
  Assigning a lambda to a property of a constructor-supplied collaborator during
  init (e.g. `transport.onClose = { onMessage(it) }`) hands the still-constructing
  object's behavior to another object before the constructor returns. If that
  collaborator invokes the callback early (or on another thread), it observes a
  half-initialized `this`. Move wiring into an explicit `start()`/`connect()`
  method called after construction. Tenet: explicit construction over magic.
  Note: `this.foo = { ... }` and bare `foo = { ... }` (own-field init) do NOT match.
  Caveat: assigning a lambda to a property of a LOCAL object built inside init
  (a builder pattern) is not a leak; treat such a warning as a false positive.
rule:
  kind: anonymous_initializer
  has:
    stopBy: end
    kind: assignment
    all:
      - has:
          kind: directly_assignable_expression
          all:
            - has:
                kind: navigation_suffix
            - not:
                has:
                  kind: this_expression
      - has:
          kind: lambda_literal

id: no-try-catch-in-init
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: try/catch inside an init block performs fallible work during construction and tends to swallow failures.
note: |
  A try/catch executed directly in init means the constructor is doing work that
  can fail (I/O, parsing, decoding) and is deciding how to recover at construction
  time — often by fabricating a fallback (`catch { "" }`), which violates the
  no-sentinel rule. Construction should be total and cheap; move fallible work
  into a suspend factory that can fail explicitly or return a typed result.
  Tenet: explicit construction over magic; no sentinel fabrication.
  (A try/catch inside a lambda/callback defined in init runs at call time, not
  construction time, and is intentionally NOT matched.)
rule:
  kind: try_expression
  inside:
    kind: anonymous_initializer
    stopBy: end
  not:
    inside:
      any:
        - kind: lambda_literal
        - kind: anonymous_function
      stopBy: end
goodExample:
class Config private constructor(val data: String)
suspend fun loadConfig(path: String): Config = Config(readFile(path)) // failure propagates

id: no-flat-lifecycle-event
language: kotlin
severity: error

# whole-tree ci-gate enforce it). The header used to say "STAGED ... activate by renaming ...
# once the 9 flat lifecycle events are converted": the redesign landed, the rename happened,
# and the prose describing the rule as inert outlived both — so a reader checking whether this
# invariant is enforced would have concluded it is not. It is.
#
# Its zero live hits are a CORRECTLY unmoved instrument, not an inert rule: Lifecycle.kt:24 and
# Streaming.kt:84 are the only event hierarchies left and both are `sealed class` with nested
# subtypes, i.e. the shape this forbids has genuinely been eliminated. The fixture proves the
# rule still fires on a flat `OnFooEvent(...)`, which is what separates zero-because-clean from
# zero-because-broken.

# Enforces: a top-level `data class …Event` MUST be a subtype of the sealed event
# hierarchy (have a `: AgentEvent()` supertype), never a free-floating flat struct.
# Tested: matches a flat `OnFooEvent(...)`; skips `… : AgentEvent()` subtypes and
# non-event data classes.

# Two holes closed after review, both of which made the wall narrower than this header claims:
#
#  1. It required `class_modifier: data`. This repo's CLAUDE.md mandates `@Poko class` over
#     `data class` for public value types, and Lifecycle.kt:29 is written exactly that way
#     (`@Poko public class Started<TContext> ... : AgentEvent()`). So the rule was blind to the
#     ONLY shape a new event would be written in under current policy — its zero was guaranteed
#     regardless of what anyone added. Now matches either idiom.
#  2. It was `not: has: delegation_specifier` — "must have SOME supertype". A flat
#     `data class OnBarEvent(...) : Serializable` satisfied that and passed, while the header
#     claimed subtyping of the sealed hierarchy. Now the supertype must actually name
#     AgentEvent/StreamEvent.
rule:
  all:
    - kind: class_declaration
    - inside: { kind: source_file }
    - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: 'Event$', stopBy: neighbor }
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        any:
          - has: { kind: class_modifier, regex: 'data' }
          - has: { kind: annotation, has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^Poko$', stopBy: end } }
    - not:
        has:
          kind: delegation_specifier
          stopBy: neighbor

            kind: type_identifier
            regex: '(AgentEvent|StreamEvent)$'

id: no-public-expect-declaration
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "A public (or non-internal) expect declaration leaks a platform bridge into the public ABI; every existing expect/actual seam in this SDK is internal."
note: >-
  expect/actual seams are platform-bridge implementation details, not
  consumer-facing API. The Kotlin compiler already enforces
  actual-exists-per-target on its own (a missing actual is a compile error,
  not something ast-grep needs to check) — but it does not enforce visibility
  discipline. All 4 existing commonMain expect declarations (SecureRandom.kt's
  SecureRandom, MCP.kt's CreateMCPStdioProcess, JvmInteropAnnotations.kt's
  AiSdkJvmStatic, AbortSignal.kt's AbortErrorCancellationBridge) are internal;
  keep new ones internal too so a platform bridge never becomes an ABI
  commitment across every target.


  GRAMMAR NOTE (measured 2026-07-25, ast-grep 0.44.0 / tree-sitter-kotlin) —
  read before adding a multi-declaration fixture here or to any expect rule.
  Consecutive top-level `expect` declarations in ONE file do not each produce a
  `modifiers` node: a bodyless declaration swallows the ones that follow it, so a
  file with three public expect declarations reports 1 match, not 3. Verified
  counts: object(bodyless)+class+fun -> 1; class+fun+object(last) -> 2;
  class+fun -> 1. This is a tree-sitter grammar limitation, not Kotlin semantics.

  It is NOT an enforcement hole, and that distinction is the point: the rule
  UNDER-COUNTS multiple violations in one file but never goes silent on a file
  that contains one. Verified in the direction that matters — a compliant
  declaration placed before a violating one (internal object then public fun;
  internal fun then public class; internal class then public fun) still reports
  the violation in every case, so a compliant declaration cannot mask a
  non-compliant one and the gate still goes red.

  Consequence for fixtures: a multi-form badExample would satisfy the validator
  (which requires >=1 match) while exercising only ONE form — coverage that reads
  as three and is one. Each form is instead verified directly: `public expect
  object`, `public expect class`, `public abstract expect class` and `public
  expect fun` each match alone; the internal/private/protected counterparts and
  ordinary public declarations each match zero times.
rule:
  kind: modifiers
  all:
    - has: { kind: platform_modifier, regex: '^expect$' }
    - not:
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'

goodExample: internal expect object AbortErrorCancellationBridge

yaml:
id: no-throwable-catch-without-rethrow
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "catch (x: Throwable) whose body never throws swallows CancellationException, breaking structured-concurrency cancellation."
note: >-
  A catch block typed on Throwable (broader than the already-flagged `catch
  (e: Exception)` in avoid-broad-catch-exception, since Throwable also spans
  Error and any non-Exception Throwable) whose body contains no `throw` at
  all converts every caught failure — including a CancellationException from
  a cancelled coroutine — into a non-throwing value (a logged warning, an
  updated state field, a returned fallback): the structured-concurrency
  unwind silently stops there instead of propagating. This repo's established
  idiom (see avoid-broad-catch-exception's and no-empty-catch-block's
  goodExamples) is `catch (ce: CancellationException) { throw ce } catch (e:
  SomeType) { ... }`, or an unconditional rethrow (wrapped or not) inside the
  Throwable catch itself; a catch parameter explicitly discarded as `_` is
  the established best-effort-ignore idiom (matches no-empty-catch-block's
  own carve-out) and is intentionally not flagged. The registry autofix inserts
  the minimal guard line as the first catch statement; the preferred handwritten
  form remains the explicit `catch (ce: CancellationException) { throw ce }`
  before the broad catch. Severity is warning, not
  error: this pattern already exists across roughly 20 call sites in
  commonMain (RetryPolicy, CompletionApi, Telemetry, SmoothStream,
  StructuredObjectApi, Generate, AbortSignal, AgentSession,
  AgentTelemetryDispatcher, ui/Streams, ToolLoopAgent, Tool, MCP,
  ToolCallRepairer, GoogleInteractionsStreamState) — the incremental hook
  grandfathers all of them and only nudges on newly introduced instances.
rule:
  kind: catch_block
  all:
    - pattern:
        context: |
          try {
            $$$TRY
          } catch ($$$CATCH_PARAM: Throwable) {
            $$$BODY
          }
        selector: catch_block
    - has:
        kind: simple_identifier
        pattern: $ERR
    - not:
        has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^_$' }
    - not:
        has: { pattern: 'throw $X', stopBy: end }
    - not:
        inside:
          kind: try_expression
          stopBy: end
          has:
            pattern:
              context: |
                try {
                  $$$TRY
                } catch ($CE: CancellationException) {
                  $$$CE_BODY
                }
              selector: catch_block
fix: |-
  catch ($$$CATCH_PARAM: Throwable) {
      CancellationExceptions.asCancellationExceptionOrNull($ERR)?.let { throw it }
      $$$BODY
  }
badExample: try { x() } catch (@Suppress("TooGenericExceptionCaught") error: Throwable) { logger.warn("x", error) }
goodExample:
try { x() } catch (error: Throwable) { if (error is CancellationException) throw error; onError(error) }

try { y() } catch (ce: CancellationException) { onError(ce) } catch (error: Throwable) { onError(error) }

id: no-runcatching-in-suspend
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "runCatching in suspend/coroutine-builder code swallows CancellationException; use explicit try/catch that rethrows cancellation."
note: >-

  NoRunCatchingInSuspendFunction. It flags stdlib runCatching under a suspend
  named function, and the type-free coroutine-builder case detekt can prove:
  runCatching inside launch/async/withContext/coroutineScope/supervisorScope
  whose body calls a suspend function declared in the same file. Detekt remains
  the blocking owner; this warning rule is the earlier feedback layer.

  all:

    - any:
        - inside:
            kind: function_declaration
            stopBy: end
            has:
              kind: modifiers
              has: { kind: function_modifier, regex: '^suspend$' }
        - all:
            - inside:
                stopBy: end
                any:
                  - pattern: '$RECEIVER.launch { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: '$RECEIVER.launch($$$BUILDER_ARGS) { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: 'launch { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: 'launch($$$BUILDER_ARGS) { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'

                  - pattern: '$RECEIVER.async($$$BUILDER_ARGS) { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: 'async { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: 'async($$$BUILDER_ARGS) { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: 'withContext($$$BUILDER_ARGS) { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'
                  - pattern: 'coroutineScope { $$$BUILDER_BODY }'

id: no-public-member-extension-in-object
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: >-
  A public extension function declared inside a public `object` forces every
  call site into a member-import or `with(Object) { ... }` block. Move the
  function onto the type it extends (a member, or a default method on its
  interface) instead.
note: >-
  This is the pattern eliminated repo-wide in 0.3.0-beta01 (ProviderModels,
  GeneratedFiles, AgentSessions, ChatSessionFactory, ToolResultOutputs,
  UsageArithmetic, UIMessageMetadata — see CHANGELOG.md "Unreleased"): a
  public member-extension parked in a public `object` is ergonomically worse
  than a member on the owning type, with no offsetting benefit — decision-C
  ("no loose top-level functions") is satisfied just as well by a member.
  Plain (non-extension) functions in a public object remain the sanctioned
  factory-namespace pattern (e.g. `AbortSignals.from(job)`); private
  member-extensions inside a class, and member-extensions inside an
  internal/private object, are implementation detail and are not flagged.
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: receiver_type
    - not:
        has:
          kind: modifiers
          has:
            kind: visibility_modifier
            regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'
    - inside:
        kind: class_body
        inside:
          kind: object_declaration
          not:
            has:
              kind: modifiers
              has:
                kind: visibility_modifier
                regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'

# TENET: No companion objects — move members to top-level declarations.
# Rationale: Companion objects hide top-level helpers behind a class body and encourage god classes.
# Every companion member can be a top-level declaration in the same file, before the class.
# Pattern: Instead of `class X { companion object { fun create() } }` use `fun createX()` at top level.
id: no-companion-objects
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "Move companion object members to top-level declarations in the same file, before the class."
files:

ignores:

# TENET: a class that constructs its own CoroutineScope must cancel it.
#
# The upstream torad-toolkit rule for this invariant is `no-coroutine-scope-factory`,
# which bans the `CoroutineScope(...)` factory outright and points at viewModelScope /
# lifecycleScope / an injected scope. That is correct for an Android app and WRONG for
# this repo: a published KMP SDK has no ambient host scope to borrow, so owning a scope
# is legitimate — the obligation is to cancel it. Verified: the upstream rule reports 6
# hits here (Generate.kt:214, ToolLoopAgent.kt:244, MCP.kt:381/1424/1774/2100), and five
# of those explicitly cancel in close(). Banning the construct would be a false positive
# five times over; requiring the cancel is the invariant that actually holds.
#
# Scope law (toolkit doctrine): exclusion only. New files are inside this law by default.
#
# Matcher: `pattern:` rather than a hand-built kind:/has: tree, per the same doctrine —
# the elaborate CST-walking version of this rule false-positived on `@CoroutineScope()`
# annotation sites, because tree-sitter parses an annotation application as
# `annotation > constructor_invocation > user_type`, structurally identical to a supertype.
# `pattern: CoroutineScope($$$ARGS)` cannot make that mistake.
#
# stopBy: end on both relations, deliberately. Both are transitive: the construction sits
# inside a property initialiser or a method body, and the matching cancel() sits in a
# different member entirely (typically close()/teardown), so neither is a direct child of
# class_declaration. Omitting stopBy makes both relations structurally unsatisfiable and
# the rule silently dead.
#
# Severity is `warning`, not error, on purpose. One site does not satisfy it today:
# Generate.kt:169 MemoizedStreamReplay constructs a scope in registerCollector and cancels
# only the Job it launched (`abandonedProducer?.cancel()`), never the scope. That is safe
# in practice — the scope is a local, its sole child is cancelled, and it is then
# collectible — but it is a real deviation. Promoting this rule to LAW (rules/) requires
# fixing that site first: hold the scope and cancel the scope, which cancels the child as
# a superset of today's behaviour.
id: coroutine-scope-must-be-cancelled
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "This class constructs a CoroutineScope but never cancels it. A self-constructed scope is owned: cancel it in close()/teardown, or take an injected scope whose lifetime the caller owns."
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
  - "**/test/**"
  - "**/*Test/**"
rule:
  kind: class_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        pattern: CoroutineScope($$$ARGS)
    # The cancel side is kind-based, NOT `pattern: $SCOPE.cancel()`. A safe call
    # `scope?.cancel()` parses as navigation_expression > navigation_suffix with a `?.`
    # token instead of `.`, so the pattern form missed it and kept flagging a class that
    # does cancel correctly. Both spellings share this shape, so matching the suffix
    # identifier covers them. Found by fixing Generate.kt and watching the rule stay red.
    - not:
        has:
          stopBy: end
          kind: call_expression
          has:
            kind: navigation_expression
            has:
              kind: navigation_suffix
              has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^cancel$' }

# TENET: NonCancellable is a withContext-only context element.
#
# NonCancellable is an already-completed Job. Passing it to launch/async makes it the new
# coroutine's PARENT job, which severs the child from its scope: the coroutine becomes both
# un-cancellable and orphaned, so nothing can ever stop it — not close(), not the scope, not
# the caller. It exists for one shape only: a bounded `withContext(NonCancellable) { ... }`
# cleanup block that must survive cancellation of the surrounding work.
#
# Scope law (toolkit doctrine): exclusion only, so new files are inside this law by default.
#
# THE CALLEE MUST BE A DIRECT CHILD — this is the whole rule. `stopBy: end` on the callee
# was measured to produce a false positive on real code: MCP.kt:2115
# `lifecycle.setReader(readerScope.launch { ... })` matched, because the OUTER setReader call
# contains a `launch` somewhere below it and, separately, a `NonCancellable` deeper inside the
# lambda body. Any enclosing call would match that way. A call's own callee is a direct child —
# `simple_identifier` for bare `launch(...)`, `navigation_expression > navigation_suffix >
# simple_identifier` for `scope.launch(...)` — so the direct-child form is both correct and
# what distinguishes "this call is a launch" from "this call contains a launch".
#
# The argument side keeps `stopBy: end`, deliberately and safely: it is scoped INSIDE
# `call_suffix > value_arguments`, and Kotlin's trailing lambda is an `annotated_lambda`, a
# SIBLING of value_arguments rather than a child. So a body-level
# `launch(Dispatchers.IO) { withContext(NonCancellable) { ... } }` — the legitimate shape,
# live at Generate.kt:202 — is structurally excluded, while `stopBy: end` still reaches
# NonCancellable through a compound `NonCancellable + handler` (additive_expression) and a
# named `context = NonCancellable` (value_argument with an identifier label).
#
# That compound form is why an earlier attempt at this rule failed review: it carried a
# `not: has: {kind: lambda_literal, stopBy: end}` guard meant to exclude the trailing lambda,
# which also suppressed every argument that merely CONTAINED a lambda — so
# `launch(NonCancellable + CoroutineExceptionHandler { ... })` went undetected while the
# simple form matched, and the rule looked like it worked. Scoping to value_arguments removes
# the need for that guard entirely.
#
# Verified: all four violating forms match (bare, compound, async, named-argument); the two
# legitimate forms and a wrapped `wrap(s.launch { withContext(NonCancellable) { } })` do not;
# 0 hits across every scanned source set.
id: no-noncancellable-in-launch
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "NonCancellable passed to launch/async makes the coroutine its own un-cancellable root — it is orphaned from its scope and nothing can stop it. Use it only as `withContext(NonCancellable) { }` around a bounded cleanup block; to start work, pass a real context (dispatcher/CoroutineName) and let the scope own cancellation."
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
  - "**/test/**"
  - "**/*Test/**"
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  all:
    - has:
        any:
          - { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(launch|async)$' }
          - kind: navigation_expression
            has:
              kind: navigation_suffix
              has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(launch|async)$' }
    - has:
        kind: call_suffix
        has:
          kind: value_arguments
          has: { stopBy: end, kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^NonCancellable$' }

# Scope law (toolkit doctrine): exclusion only — new files are inside this law by default.

# alternative in a regex alternation that suppressed genuine findings, and it still missed
# awaitClose misplaced inside a nested `launch { }`. Those are two different invariants, so
# they are two rules — this one owns PRESENCE, and no-awaitclose-inside-coroutine-builder
# owns PLACEMENT. Each is simple enough to verify in both directions.

# The `not:` uses stopBy: end deliberately: awaitClose is legitimately wrapped (a try/finally
# around it is idiomatic, and the repo would flag that as a false positive if the search were
# depth-limited). Placement is not this rule's business — the companion rule owns it — so
# searching the whole subtree is correct here rather than lenient.
#
# Verified: a callbackFlow with no awaitClose matches; one with a direct awaitClose does not;
# one with awaitClose inside try/finally does not; one with awaitClose nested in launch does
# not match THIS rule (it is the companion rule's finding, not a miss). 0 hits in the repo —

language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "This callbackFlow never calls awaitClose. Collection throws IllegalStateException, or the registered callback is never unregistered on cancellation and leaks for the process lifetime. End the producer block with awaitClose { /* unregister */ }."
ignores:

  - "**/test/**"

          kind: call_expression

# awaitClose suspends until the channel is closed and then runs its teardown. Nested inside
# `launch { }` or `async { }` it suspends the CHILD coroutine instead of the producer block,

# `!scope.isClosedForSend` check then fires — the exact failure awaitClose exists to prevent,
# reached by code that appears to call it. This is the classic callbackFlow mistake and it
# reads as correct in review.

# Scope law (toolkit doctrine): exclusion only — new files are inside this law by default.

# Companion to no-callbackflow-without-awaitclose, which owns PRESENCE while this owns
# PLACEMENT. Splitting them is what makes each verifiable: a single matcher trying to express
# both missed this case entirely while also suppressing real findings through a regex
# alternation. Not a dedupe violation — disjoint predicates, and a block can fail either one
# independently (present-but-misplaced fails only this rule; absent fails only the other).
#
# stopBy: end on the `inside:` is required and safe. Required because launch/async sit
# arbitrarily deep — inside a `let`, a `forEach`, a `try` — so the relation is genuinely

# directly in the producer block has no launch/async ancestor at all, so it cannot match.

# Verified: awaitClose inside `launch { }` matches; a direct awaitClose does not; awaitClose
# inside try/finally does not. 0 hits in the repo — preventive.
id: no-awaitclose-inside-coroutine-builder
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "awaitClose is nested inside launch/async, so it suspends that child coroutine instead of the callbackFlow producer block — the producer returns immediately and the callback still leaks. Call awaitClose directly in the producer block."
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
  - "**/test/**"
  - "**/*Test/**"
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^awaitClose$' }
  inside:
    stopBy: end
    kind: call_expression
    has:
      any:
        - { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(launch|async)$' }
        - kind: navigation_expression
          has:

            has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(launch|async)$' }

# TENET: every emission from a `flow { }` builder must happen in the collector's own context.
#
# `flow { }` hands the block a SafeCollector that records the CoroutineContext it was collected
# in and re-checks it on every emit. Starting a coroutine inside the block — withContext,
# launch, async — installs a different context, so the emission fails that check with
# `IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated: emission from another coroutine`. The
# compiler cannot see it; it is a runtime crash on the streaming path.
#
# Fixes: hoist the switch off the emission (`val v = withContext(io) { read() }; emit(v)`),
# move the whole upstream with `.flowOn(dispatcher)`, or use `channelFlow { send(v) }`, whose
# send is designed for concurrent emission.
#
# Scope law (toolkit doctrine): exclusion only — new files are inside this law by default.
#
# THE NEAREST-BOUNDARY WALK IS THE RULE. Two prior attempts were refuted as WOULD_MISFIRE
# because they searched for an ancestor rather than the NEAREST one, and so flagged five
# legitimate shapes. `stopBy:` takes a RULE here, not `end`: walk up from the emission and
# halt at the first coroutine builder OR flow builder, then require that boundary to be a
# coroutine builder. flow/channelFlow/callbackFlow appear in the stopBy set purely as
# TERMINATORS — they are deliberately absent from the sibling `any:` — so hitting one first
# means "the nearest collector is a legal one" and the rule correctly declines.
#
# That single mechanism is what makes all five previously-misfiring shapes pass:
#   hoisted    `val v = withContext(io) { read() }; emit(v)`  -> emit's nearest is flow
#   flowOn     `flow { emit(x) }.flowOn(io)`                  -> emit's nearest is flow
#   channelFlow`channelFlow { launch { send(x) } }`           -> send, and channelFlow terminates
#   collect    `up.collect { emit(it) }`                      -> collect is not a boundary
#   cleanup    `try { emit(x) } finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { close() } }`
#                                                             -> the cleanup block has no emit
# The last is live at Generate.kt:202 and is correct code; flagging it was the sharpest of
# the earlier false positives.
#
# The inner `inside:` uses stopBy: end because THAT relation is genuinely transitive: the
# context switch sits arbitrarily deep inside the builder (in a try, a while, a forEach).
# Over-reach there is already neutralised by the nearest-boundary walk above it.
#
# Verified: both violating shapes match (withContext-wrapped emit, launch-wrapped emit); all
# five compliant shapes above do not; 0 hits across 264 emit/flow references in the repo.
id: no-emit-in-coroutine-builder-inside-flow
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "emit/emitAll runs inside a coroutine builder (withContext/launch/async) while its FlowCollector belongs to an enclosing flow { }. The SafeCollector rejects emission from another coroutine: IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated. Hoist the context switch off the emission, use .flowOn(...), or switch to channelFlow { send(...) }."
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
  - "**/test/**"
  - "**/*Test/**"
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(emit|emitAll)$' }
  inside:
    stopBy:
      any:
        - kind: call_expression
          has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(withContext|launch|async|flow|channelFlow|callbackFlow)$' }
    kind: call_expression
    has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(withContext|launch|async)$' }
    inside:
      stopBy: end
      kind: call_expression
      has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^flow$' }

# TENET: a manual source-set refines edge requires applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate().
#
# Declaring an intermediate source set by hand (`val jvmAndAndroidMain by creating { ... }`,
# or `sourceSets.create(...)` + `getByName(...).dependsOn(...)`) silently switches OFF Kotlin's
# auto-applied default hierarchy template for the WHOLE project. Every source set the template
# would have created — nativeMain, appleMain, iosMain — stops existing, and the failure surfaces
# as unresolved references in platform code far from the edit that caused it.
#
# Scope law (toolkit doctrine): exclusion only — new files are inside this law by default.
#
# AST, NOT TEXT. This was specified as a python detector parsing build.gradle.kts, and every
# adversarial objection against it was a text-parsing artifact: plugin markers vanishing when
# string literals were stripped, and `dependsOn` matching in contexts that are not source-set
# edges at all. build.gradle.kts IS Kotlin and ast-grep parses .kts, so the AST answers both
# for free. This repo's own build has `dependsOn(...)` at lines 239/255/303-306/338 inside
# `tasks.register` and `tasks.named` blocks — a text scan sees five false edges; anchoring the
# search inside the `kotlin { }` call_expression sees none of them.
#
# Both callee shapes are enumerated on purpose. A bare `dependsOn(x)` is a direct
# simple_identifier child, while `sourceSets.getByName("jvmMain").dependsOn(x)` puts it under
# navigation_expression > navigation_suffix. Matching only the bare form MISSED the entire
# explicit-container idiom — a one-hop, semantics-preserving refactor of this repo's own build
# — which is precisely the missed-violation class that the oracle cannot detect. The same
# alternation is applied to applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate so a qualified `this.apply...()` is
# not read as absent, which would be a false positive in the opposite direction.
#
# stopBy: end on both inner relations, deliberately: the refines edge and the template call sit
# at arbitrary depth inside the kotlin block (inside sourceSets { }, inside a val initialiser,
# inside a targets loop). Omitting stopBy makes both structurally unsatisfiable and the rule
# silently dead. Over-reach is bounded by the outer anchor being the `kotlin { }` block itself.
#
# Verified on six shapes: a compliant KMP build with NO manual edge does not match (KGP applies
# the template automatically there — the sharpest false positive in review); `by creating` and
# `sourceSets.create` both match when the template is absent; bare and qualified template calls
# both suppress; and the repo's real build.gradle.kts, which is compliant at lines 146 and 154,
# returns 0.

language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "This kotlin { } block declares a manual source-set refines edge but never calls applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate(). The manual edge disables the default hierarchy project-wide, so nativeMain/appleMain/iosMain stop existing and platform code fails to resolve. Add applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate()."
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  all:
    - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^kotlin$' }
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: call_expression
        has:
          any:
            - { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^dependsOn$' }
            - kind: navigation_expression
              has:
                kind: navigation_suffix
                has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^dependsOn$' }
    - not:
        has:
          stopBy: end
          kind: call_expression
          has:
            any:
              - { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate$' }
              - kind: navigation_expression
                has:
                  kind: navigation_suffix
                  has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^applyDefaultHierarchyTemplate$' }

# is warning rather than error until that lands.
id: no-reflection-in-production
language: kotlin
severity: warning
# Scope law: exclude-based only — new files/folders are inside this law by default.
# Promoted from torad-fleet (2026-07-13, CR-TOOLKIT-PROMOTE); this pack is the clean
# canonical form — see sgconfig.yml for the full exclude-scope doctrine banner.
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
  - "**/node_modules/**"
  - "**/dist/**"
  - "**/*.gradle.kts"
  - "**/src/*Test/kotlin/**"
  - "**/src/test/kotlin/**"

message: "no-reflection-in-production: avoid reflection. Use interfaces, generics, or sealed types instead."

badExample: internal fun retryable(t: Throwable): Boolean = t::class.qualifiedName == "java.io.IOException"

yaml:
id: no-deprecated-without-version
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "`@Deprecated` message doesn't mention a version. Without a version, consumers can't tell how urgent the migration is or when the symbol will be removed. Mention the version it was deprecated in and/or the version it will be removed in, e.g. `@Deprecated(\"Use X instead, removed in 2.0.0\")`."
# Bind only the first deprecation argument (the message). A relational stopBy:end walk
# previously matched ANY nested string — including ReplaceWith("newApi()") — so a
# compliant declaration still warned. Pattern metavariable $MESSAGE is the first arg only.
rule:
  any:
    - pattern: '@Deprecated($MESSAGE)'
    - pattern: '@Deprecated($MESSAGE, $$$REST)'
constraints:
  MESSAGE:
    not:
      regex: '(?i)(version|\d+\.\d+)'
badExample:
@Deprecated("Use newApi instead", ReplaceWith("newApi()"))
public fun oldApi(): Int = 1
goodExample:
@Deprecated("Use newApi instead, removed in 2.0.0", ReplaceWith("newApi()"))
public fun oldApi(): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-public-without-since
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public declaration has no KDoc `@since` tag (either no KDoc at all, or a KDoc missing `@since`). This is a published, ABI-validated library — consumers and changelog tooling rely on `@since` to know which release introduced a symbol. Add a `/** ... @since X.Y.Z */` block directly above the declaration."
note: |
  Require the KDoc opening token (`/**`). A plain block comment `/* @since ... */` is NOT
  published by Dokka, so accepting any multiline_comment let non-KDoc markers slip through.

  Two exemption shapes, both measured against this tree:

  1. A KDoc written AFTER an annotation is not a preceding sibling — tree-sitter places it inside
     the declaration's own `modifiers` node, between the annotation and the visibility modifier.
     The repo's dominant public-API style is annotation-first (`@Poko`, `@Serializable`,
     `@JvmSynthetic`, `@OptIn`), so without the `has: modifiers` clause this rule fired on exactly
     the documented style CLAUDE.md requires.
  2. A `public` member of a private/internal class or object is not public API and needs no marker.

  KNOWN RESIDUAL: when a long `/** ... */` doc block is stacked directly above the
  `/** @since */` line, ast-grep's `follows` does not see the marker and this still warns (26 sites
  on this tree). Every formulation that closes it (`stopBy: end`, a `stopBy` rule, nested `follows`)
  over-matches instead and exempts the ENTIRE tree — 0 hits — which would be silent false negatives
  rather than noise. The blocking owner of this invariant is
  `tools/check-public-api-since-budget.mjs`, which uses a 12-line lookback and therefore handles
  both shapes correctly; it reports 0 missing. This rule is the edit-time mirror, so it is left
  noisy-but-safe rather than made quiet-and-wrong.
rule:
  all:
    - any:
        - kind: function_declaration
        - kind: class_declaration
        - kind: property_declaration
        - kind: object_declaration
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has: { kind: visibility_modifier, regex: '^public$' }
    - not:
        any:
          - follows:
              kind: multiline_comment
              regex: '^/\*\*[\s\S]*@since'
          - has:
              kind: modifiers
              has:
                kind: multiline_comment
                regex: '^/\*\*[\s\S]*@since'
    - not:
        inside:
          stopBy: end
          any:
            - kind: class_declaration
            - kind: object_declaration
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has: { kind: visibility_modifier, regex: '^(private|internal)$' }
badExample:
/* @since 0.3.0-beta01 */
public fun notKdoc(): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-any-in-public-signature
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Any/Any? used as a parameter or return type on a public function erases type information from the API — callers have to unsafe-cast it back to something useful. Use a concrete type, a reified/generic type parameter, or a sealed hierarchy instead of Any/Any?."
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^public$'
    - any:
        - has:
            kind: function_value_parameters
            has:
              kind: parameter
              has:
                any:
                  - all:
                      - kind: user_type
                      - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^Any$' }
                  - all:
                      - kind: nullable_type
                      - has:
                          kind: user_type
                          has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^Any$' }
        - has:
            any:
              - all:
                  - kind: user_type
                  - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^Any$' }
                  - follows: { kind: function_value_parameters, stopBy: end }
              - all:
                  - kind: nullable_type
                  - has:
                      kind: user_type
                      has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^Any$' }
                  - follows: { kind: function_value_parameters, stopBy: end }
badExample: public fun handle(value: Any): Int = 1
goodExample: public fun handle(value: String): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-callback-style-api
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public function takes a callback/listener parameter; prefer a suspend function or a Flow-returning function over a Java-style callback."
note: |
  Flags a non-suspend, non-Flow-returning, publicly-visible function that
  declares a parameter named like a callback (`onXxx`, `callback`,
  `listener`, case-insensitive) or typed as a `*Callback`/`*Listener`. This
  is a naming-convention heuristic, not a generic "no lambda parameters"
  rule: ordinary higher-order functions (`map { }`, a DSL builder lambda
  named `block`) are intentionally NOT flagged — only the callback/listener
  naming shape is. `suspend` functions, `private`/`internal`/`protected`
  functions, and functions that already return `Flow<T>` are excluded, since
  those are the target replacement shapes, not the anti-pattern.
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - not:
        has:
          kind: modifiers
          has:
            kind: function_modifier
            regex: '^suspend$'
    - not:
        has:
          kind: modifiers
          has:
            kind: visibility_modifier
            regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'
    - not:
        has:
          kind: user_type
          has:
            kind: type_identifier
            regex: '^Flow$'
    - has:
        kind: function_value_parameters
        has:
          kind: parameter
          all:
            - any:
                - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '(?i)^(on[A-Z]\w*|callback|listener)$' }
                - has: { kind: user_type, has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '(Callback|Listener)$' } }
            - not: { regex: '\bsuspend\b' }
badExample: public fun load(onDone: (String) -> Unit) { onDone("") }
goodExample: public suspend fun load(): String = ""

yaml:
id: no-channel-in-public-api
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public function takes or returns a kotlinx.coroutines.Channel. Channel is a low-level primitive with close/cancel/backpressure semantics that leak implementation details once they're in a public signature, and (like Flow) it has no natural Java/Swift interop shape. Expose a Flow (for a read-only stream consumers collect) or a suspend function instead, and keep the Channel itself private to the implementation."
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^public$'
    - any:
        - has:
            kind: user_type
            all:
              - has:
                  kind: type_identifier
                  regex: '^Channel$'
                  stopBy: end
              - not:
                  precedes:
                    regex: '^\.$'
        - has:
            kind: function_value_parameters
            has:
              kind: parameter
              has:
                kind: user_type
                has:
                  kind: type_identifier
                  regex: '^Channel$'
                  stopBy: end
badExample: public fun events(): Channel<String> = TODO()
goodExample: public fun events(): Flow<String> = TODO()

yaml:
id: no-companion-factory-without-invoke
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Companion object exposes a create()/of()/from() factory without an `operator fun invoke`; add `operator fun invoke(...)` so callers can construct with `Type(...)` instead of `Type.create(...)`."
note: |
  General Kotlin idiom: a companion `operator fun invoke` lets callers write
  `Type(args)` instead of `Type.create(args)`/`Type.of(args)`, which reads
  like ordinary construction. This repo's own construct-type convention
  (see CLAUDE.md's builder/DSL pattern, e.g. `CohereProviderSettings { ... }`)
  already achieves the same "looks like construction" ergonomic via a
  top-level PascalCase factory FUNCTION rather than a companion `invoke` —
  that pattern does not trip this rule (it has no companion `create`/`of`/
  `from`). This rule targets the specific shape of a companion object that
  chose the create/of/from naming without also adding invoke; it does not
  mandate invoke over this repo's established DSL-factory convention.
rule:
  kind: companion_object
  all:
    - has:
        kind: class_body
        has:
          kind: function_declaration
          has:
            kind: simple_identifier
            regex: '^(create|of|from)$'
    - not:
        has:
          kind: class_body
          has:
            kind: function_declaration
            all:
              - has:
                  kind: simple_identifier
                  regex: '^invoke$'
              - has:
                  kind: modifiers
                  has:
                    kind: function_modifier
                    regex: '^operator$'

id: no-deprecated-without-replacewith
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "@Deprecated is missing ReplaceWith — add ReplaceWith(\"...\") so IDEs can auto-migrate callers, or explain why no mechanical replacement exists."
rule:
  kind: annotation
  all:
    - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^Deprecated$', stopBy: end }
    - not:
        has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^ReplaceWith$', stopBy: end }
badExample:
@Deprecated("Gone in 2.0.0")
public fun old(): Int = 1
goodExample:
@Deprecated("Gone in 2.0.0", ReplaceWith("newer()"))
public fun old(): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-direct-koin-get-in-class
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Direct Koin `get()`/`inject()` call inside a class body (property initializer, delegate, or method). This is the service-locator anti-pattern — dependencies resolved this way are invisible to the constructor signature and untestable without a running Koin container. Declare the dependency as a constructor parameter and wire it in the `module { }` DSL instead."
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  all:
    - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(get|inject)$' }
    - has: { kind: call_suffix }
    - inside: { kind: class_body, stopBy: end }
    - not:
        inside:
          stopBy: end
          kind: call_expression
          has:
            kind: simple_identifier
            regex: '^(module|single|factory|scoped|viewModel|factoryOf|singleOf|worker)$'
note: >-
  Name-based (matches identifiers literally named `get`/`inject` called as a
  function) since ast-grep does not resolve imports — a locally-declared function
  also named `get()`/`inject()` would false-positive. The module-DSL exclusion
  walks all enclosing call_expressions, not just the immediate one, so a `get()`
  nested inside `single { OtherImpl(get()) }` is correctly excluded even though
  it's several calls deep.
goodExample: internal class Service(private val dep: Repo)

yaml:
id: no-either-without-fold
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Reading `.left`/`.right` directly assumes which branch is present; prefer `fold`/`map`/`getOrElse` so both branches are handled explicitly."
note: |
  Flags a property read shaped `$X.left` / `$X.right` (an `Either`/`Result`-
  style discriminated union accessed positionally instead of exhaustively).
  Structural matching cannot see declared types, so this is a name-based
  heuristic: `.left()`/`.right()` method calls are excluded (different
  shape: `navigation_expression` wrapped in a `call_expression` with a
  `call_suffix`), and assignment targets (`x.left = value`) are excluded
  (Kotlin parses those as `directly_assignable_expression`, not
  `navigation_expression`, so they never reach this rule). A type that
  legitimately has `left`/`right` fields (e.g. a UI/geometry rect or
  margin/padding holder) will false-positive here; that is expected for a
  name-only heuristic — suppress or ignore such call sites.
rule:
  kind: navigation_expression
  all:
    - has:
        kind: navigation_suffix
        has:
          kind: simple_identifier
          regex: '^(left|right)$'
    - not:
        inside:
          kind: call_expression
          stopBy: neighbor
          has:
            kind: call_suffix
            stopBy: neighbor
goodExample: internal fun read(e: Either): Int = e.fold({ 0 }, { 1 })

yaml:
id: no-experimental-without-optin
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Class/function name reads as Experimental/Preview but carries no @RequiresOptIn. If this IS the opt-in marker annotation class, add @RequiresOptIn to it; otherwise annotate it with the project's opt-in marker so consumers must explicitly acknowledge the instability."
rule:
  any:
    - kind: class_declaration
      all:
        - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '(Experimental|Preview)' }
        - not:
            has:
              kind: modifiers
              has:
                kind: annotation
                has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(RequiresOptIn|Experimental[A-Za-z0-9_]*Api)$', stopBy: end }
    - kind: function_declaration
      all:
        - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '(Experimental|Preview)' }
        - not:
            has:
              kind: modifiers
              has:
                kind: annotation
                has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(RequiresOptIn|Experimental[A-Za-z0-9_]*Api)$', stopBy: end }
badExample: public class ExperimentalFeature
goodExample:
@RequiresOptIn
public annotation class ExperimentalFeature

yaml:
id: no-extension-on-platform-type
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Extension function receiver is a Java platform type (nullability unknown to Kotlin) declared without `?`; a Java caller can pass null and crash inside the extension. Mark the receiver nullable (`Date?`) and handle null explicitly."
note: |
  Kotlin cannot spell "platform type" in source (it is the compiler's
  internal `T!` for a value whose nullness Kotlin can't verify because it
  came from Java); this rule is a structural proxy that flags an extension
  function whose receiver type resolves to a well-known JDK class — either
  referenced by FQN (`java.util.Date`, detected via a `java` segment in the
  receiver's `user_type`) or by a curated list of common ambiguous-null JDK
  types (Date, File, BigDecimal, UUID, Optional, Thread, ...) — declared
  without the explicit `?` Kotlin uses to force a null check. A receiver
  already written `Date?` is excluded (the nullable case parses as
  `nullable_type` wrapping `user_type`, a different direct child of
  `receiver_type`, so it never matches `has: kind: user_type`). Kotlin
  stdlib-aliased types (`String`, `Int`, ...) are not in the curated list
  and are unaffected.
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  has:
    field: receiver
    kind: receiver_type
    has:
      kind: user_type
      any:
        - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^java$' }
        - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(Date|File|BigDecimal|BigInteger|UUID|Pattern|Optional|Thread|Random|Scanner|Properties|Calendar|TimeZone|URL|URI|Locale|Matcher)$' }
badExample: internal fun File.sizeKb(): Int = 1
goodExample: internal fun String.sizeKb(): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-flow-collect-in-init
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "`.collect` inside init starts flow collection during construction, before the instance has a lifecycle-scoped CoroutineScope to cancel it with. Start collection from an explicit start()/onCreate() method instead."
note: |
  Matches `.collect { ... }` and `.collect(...)` anywhere under an init
  block (including inside a `launch { }`/`async { }` started in init, which
  is the common real-world shape of this bug: the coroutine is scheduled as
  a direct effect of construction, before the caller ever gets a reference
  to cancel it). A `.collect` inside a lambda that is merely assigned to a
  property for later invocation (a stored callback, not an
  immediately-scheduled coroutine builder) is a narrower false-positive
  risk this heuristic does not special-case; treat such a hit as a false
  positive. Tenet: explicit construction over magic (construction should
  not have side effects that outlive the constructor call).
rule:
  kind: anonymous_initializer
  has:
    stopBy: end
    any:
      - pattern: $FLOW.collect { $$$BODY }
      - pattern: $FLOW.collect($$$ARGS)

id: no-flow-return-without-wrapper
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public function returns Flow<...> directly. kotlinx.coroutines.Flow has no stable ABI for Java/Swift/Obj-C consumers of this KMP library — a raw Flow in the public surface forces every non-Kotlin caller to hand-roll a collector. Provide (or pair this with) a blocking/callback-friendly wrapper — a suspend function returning the terminal value, a listener-based API, or a platform-specific bridge — instead of exposing Flow as the only entry point."
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        all:
          - has:
              kind: visibility_modifier
              regex: '^public$'
          # Exclude functions already marked @JvmSynthetic (hidden from Java)
          - not:
              has:
                kind: annotation
                has:
                  kind: user_type
                  has:
                    kind: type_identifier
                    regex: '^JvmSynthetic$'
    - has:
        kind: user_type
        all:
          - has:
              kind: type_identifier
              regex: '^Flow$'
          - follows:
              kind: function_value_parameters
              stopBy: end
badExample: public fun stream(): Flow<String> = TODO()
goodExample:
@JvmSynthetic
public fun stream(): Flow<String> = TODO()

yaml:
id: no-hardcoded-baseurl
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "A URL literal is hardcoded directly into HTTP client setup (a `baseUrl`-shaped property, or an argument to `url(...)`/`host(...)`). Hardcoding the endpoint bypasses any configurable settings surface (e.g. a provider's `baseURL` builder property) and forces a recompile to point at a different environment (staging, a proxy, a self-hosted instance). Make it a constructor/builder parameter with the literal only as its default."
rule:
  kind: string_literal
  all:
    - has: { kind: string_content, regex: '^https?://' }
    - inside:
        stopBy: end
        any:
          - kind: call_expression
            has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '(?i)^(url|host|baseurl)$' }
          - kind: property_declaration
            has:
              kind: variable_declaration
              has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '(?i)(base.?url|endpoint|apiurl)' }
badExample: internal val baseUrl: String = "https://api.example.com"
goodExample: internal val baseUrl: String = readConfigValue()

yaml:
# Broader superset of `no-hardcoded-dispatcher-in-builder.yaml` (which only catches
# Dispatchers.$D as a direct argument to withContext/launch/async). This rule catches ANY
# other direct reference — property initializers, val assignments, non-builder call sites —
# while excluding the sanctioned injection pattern this package's own message recommends:
# a CoroutineContext/CoroutineDispatcher parameter defaulted to Dispatchers.$D
# (`context: CoroutineContext = Dispatchers.Default`), for both plain functions and
# constructor parameters. Running both rules together will double-report the builder-call
# case; that's expected overlap between a narrow and a broad tenet, not silent duplication.
id: no-hardcoded-dispatcher
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Hardcoded Dispatchers.IO/Main/Default reference; inject a CoroutineContext/CoroutineDispatcher parameter instead so callers (and tests) can supply their own."
rule:
  kind: navigation_expression
  all:
    - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^Dispatchers$' }
    - has:
        kind: navigation_suffix
        has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(IO|Main|Default)$' }
  not:
    any:
      - inside: { kind: function_value_parameters }
      - inside: { kind: class_parameter }
badExample: internal suspend fun load(): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { 1 }
goodExample: internal suspend fun load(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher): Int = withContext(dispatcher) { 1 }

id: no-jvmoverloads-on-expect
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "@JvmOverloads on an expect declaration has no effect — expect declares only a signature with no body, so there's no bytecode to generate overloads for. Move @JvmOverloads to the actual implementation(s) that need it."
rule:
  kind: modifiers
  all:
    - has:
        kind: annotation
        has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^JvmOverloads$', stopBy: end }
    - has: { kind: platform_modifier, regex: '^expect$' }
badExample:
@JvmOverloads
expect fun build(a: Int)
goodExample:
@JvmOverloads
fun build(a: Int) { }

  kind: modifiers

yaml:
id: no-kdoc-todo
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "KDoc contains a TODO/FIXME marker; user-facing docs must not carry unresolved work items."
note: |
  Matches a `/** ... */` (KDoc) comment whose text contains TODO or FIXME.
  Kotlin's grammar has one comment kind for both KDoc and plain block
  comments (`multiline_comment`), so the rule anchors on the leading `/**`
  to distinguish KDoc from a plain `/* ... */` block comment; `//` line
  comments never match either way. A TODO/FIXME in KDoc ships to consumers
  via generated docs (Dokka); track the work item in an issue tracker and
  either remove the marker or state the constraint as a fact ("Currently
  limited to X") instead of a to-do.
rule:
  kind: multiline_comment
  regex: '^/\*\*[\s\S]*(TODO|FIXME)'
badExample:
/** TODO: document this properly. */
public fun f(): Int = 1
goodExample:
/** Returns one. */
public fun f(): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-lateinit-in-data-class
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "lateinit var inside a data class breaks the generated equals/hashCode/toString/copy before the property is initialized; prefer a constructor parameter or a non-data holder."
note: |
  `lateinit var` is already banned everywhere by the blocking LAW rule
  `no-lateinit-var` (severity error). This style rule is a narrower,
  data-class-specific companion that exists purely for its message: it
  names the extra hazard a `data class` adds on top of the general
  lateinit risk — the compiler-generated `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString`/
  `copy` all read the property, so any call into them before the lateinit
  var is set throws `UninitializedPropertyAccessException` from generated
  code the author never wrote. In this repo the LAW rule already makes
  this specific shape unreachable in committed code; keep this rule for
  the more precise diagnostic message if `no-lateinit-var` is ever loosened
  to allow lateinit in ordinary classes.
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has:
          kind: member_modifier
          regex: '^lateinit$'
    - inside:
        kind: class_body
        inside:
          kind: class_declaration
          stopBy: neighbor
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: class_modifier
              regex: '^data$'

id: no-many-params-without-builder
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Class constructor has 5 or more parameters. A long positional parameter list is error-prone at call sites (easy to transpose two same-typed args) and freezes a wide surface into the ABI the moment it's public. Front construction with a DSL builder instead: a private-var-backed Builder class with public setter methods + an internal primary constructor + a factory function (see CLAUDE.md's construct-type pattern), so fields can be added later without breaking callers."
note: |
  The message argues an ABI consequence ("freezes a wide surface into the ABI the moment it's
  public"), so the rule now CHECKS that: the visibility clauses below mirror the sibling rule
  `no-public-constructor-with-defaults`. Without them this matched any run of 5+ class parameters
  with no visibility test at all, firing on internal constructors already fronted by the sanctioned
  builder pattern, on private data classes, and on test code — places where the stated consequence
  cannot occur.
rule:
  all:
    - kind: class_parameter
      follows:
        kind: class_parameter
        stopBy: end
        follows:
          kind: class_parameter
          stopBy: end
          follows:
            kind: class_parameter
            stopBy: end
            follows:
              kind: class_parameter
              stopBy: end
    # A non-public parameter is not part of the public surface.
    - not:
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'
          stopBy: end
    # An internal/private primary constructor is exactly the sanctioned construct-type pattern.
    - inside:
        kind: primary_constructor
        not:
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: visibility_modifier
              regex: '^(private|internal)$'
    # ...and a non-public class has no public ABI to freeze.
    - inside:
        stopBy: end
        kind: class_declaration
        not:
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: visibility_modifier
              regex: '^(private|internal)$'
badExample: public class C(val a: Int, val b: Int, val c: Int, val d: Int, val e: Int)

language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public function returns MutableList/MutableMap/MutableSet directly. Callers can mutate what you handed them behind your back, breaking any invariant the producer relied on. Return the read-only interface (List/Map/Set) and keep the mutable backing collection private to the function or class."

  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^public$'
    - has:
        kind: user_type
        all:
          - has:
              kind: type_identifier

yaml:
id: no-nullable-in-sealed-error
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "A variant of a sealed Result/Error hierarchy carries a nullable payload field. If this variant exists, the payload is presumably always present — a nullable type here means the illegal state (variant present, payload absent) is still representable. Make the field non-null, or split into variants that don't need it."
rule:
  kind: class_parameter
  all:
    - has: { kind: nullable_type }
    - inside:
        kind: primary_constructor
        inside:
          kind: class_declaration
          any:
            - has:
                kind: delegation_specifier
                has:
                  kind: constructor_invocation
                  has:
                    kind: user_type
                    has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '(?i)(result|error)' }
            - inside:
                kind: class_body
                inside:
                  kind: class_declaration
                  has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '(?i)(result|error)' }
note: >-
  Matches both shapes: a variant nested inside the sealed type's own class_body
  (`sealed class ResultX { data class Failure(val error: String?) : ResultX() }`)
  and a variant declared as a top-level sibling delegating to it
  (`data class Failure(val error: String?) : ResultX()`). Naming-based (Result/Error
  in the sealed type's identifier) since ast-grep does not resolve `sealed`-ness
  across files.
badExample: public class LoadFailure(val cause: String?) : AppError()
goodExample: public class LoadFailure(val cause: String) : AppError()

yaml:
# Broader than the LAW rule `rules/no-java-import.yaml` (which bans `import java.$$$`
# everywhere, all source sets). This style tenet additionally covers javax./android./dalvik.
# and is scoped to commonMain specifically — those packages don't exist on JS/wasm/Native
# targets, so importing them there is a compile error, not just a style nit.
id: no-platform-import-in-common
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Platform-specific import (java./javax./android./dalvik.) in commonMain — these packages don't exist on JS/wasm/Native targets. Move the platform-specific code behind an expect/actual seam."
# Scope by EXCLUSION, not a `files:` allowlist. Two reasons, both load-bearing:
#   1. A narrow `files:` glob can never match the validator's fixture, which is written to a
#      random temp path — so the rule could not be given a fixture at all, and went
#      unvalidated in both directions.
#   2. New source sets land inside the law by default instead of silently escaping it.
# java/javax/android imports are legitimate in the JVM/Android source sets; everywhere else
# (commonMain, commonTest, nativeMain) they do not exist on Native/JS and are a compile error.
ignores:
  - "**/build/**"
  - "src/jvmAndAndroidMain/**"
  - "src/jvmTest/**"
rule:
  any:
    # NAMED multi-metavariables. With the anonymous `$$$` these four patterns matched
    # NOTHING — the rule installed clean, kept the gate green, and enforced nothing. Found
    # while writing its first fixture: `import java.io.File` scored 0 matches.
    - pattern: import java.$$$REST
    - pattern: import javax.$$$REST
    - pattern: import android.$$$REST
    - pattern: import dalvik.$$$REST
badExample: import java.io.File
goodExample: import kotlin.jvm.JvmSynthetic

yaml:
id: no-primitive-amount
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Parameter named `amount`/`price`/`duration` is typed as a raw Long/Double/Int. A bare primitive carries no unit or currency, so callers can pass cents where dollars were expected, or milliseconds where seconds were expected, and the compiler won't catch it. Wrap it in a value class that encodes the unit (e.g. `@JvmInline value class Cents(val value: Long)`, `@JvmInline value class Duration(val millis: Long)`, or `kotlin.time.Duration` for durations)."
rule:
  kind: parameter
  all:
    - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(amount|price|duration)$' }
    - has:
        kind: user_type
        has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(Long|Double|Int)$' }
badExample: internal fun pay(amount: Long) { }
goodExample: internal fun pay(amount: Money) { }

yaml:
id: no-public-const-val-object
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "const val inside a public object is inlined at every call site (not a companion — those are exempt). Bumping the value later doesn't take effect for already-compiled callers until they recompile — a silent binary-compat trap for a public constant."
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has: { kind: property_modifier, regex: '^const$' }
    - inside:
        kind: class_body
        inside:
          kind: object_declaration
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has: { kind: visibility_modifier, regex: '^public$' }

id: no-public-constructor-with-defaults
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public class has a public constructor parameter with a default value. A public positional constructor with defaults freezes the parameter list into the ABI: appending, reordering, or removing a defaulted param is binary-incompatible for already-compiled callers, and @JvmOverloads/default-args don't rescue it. Front construction with a builder/DSL factory instead (internal constructor + Builder class + factory function) so the constructor itself is never part of the public contract. `@Poko` classes are exempt: CLAUDE.md settles that produced read-only types keep a public positional constructor."
note: |
  The `@Poko` exemption is not a loophole — it is the repo's settled decision (CLAUDE.md, dated
  2026-07-03, `docs/reports/pre-beta-abi-audit.md` F1): produced read-only `@Poko` types
  intentionally keep a PUBLIC positional constructor, because `@Poko` omits `copy()`/`componentN()`
  and appending a field is compatible for every READ site, which is all a consumer does with a
  produced type. Without this clause the rule fired on the very pattern the project mandates —
  result/response/usage types such as `StreamEvent` and `TranscriptSegment` — which trains
  dismissal of the whole style pack. Construct-types, which consumers BUILD, still use an
  `internal constructor` + builder and are still covered here.
rule:
  kind: class_parameter
  all:
    - has:
        follows:
          any:
            - kind: user_type
            - kind: nullable_type
    - not:
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'
          stopBy: end
    - inside:
        kind: primary_constructor
        not:
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: visibility_modifier
              regex: '^(private|internal)$'
    - inside:
        stopBy: end
        kind: class_declaration
        not:
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: visibility_modifier
              regex: '^(private|internal)$'
    - not:
        inside:
          stopBy: end
          kind: class_declaration
          has:
            kind: modifiers
            has:
              kind: annotation
              regex: '^@Poko$'
badExample: public class C(val a: Int = 1)

id: no-public-inline-calling-internal
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Public inline fun found — inline function bodies are copied into every call site, so any internal/private member they reference must be @PublishedApi (or the reference is a compile error at the call site's module boundary). Manually verify this body doesn't reach for an internal declaration without @PublishedApi."
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  has:
    kind: modifiers
    all:
      - has: { kind: visibility_modifier, regex: '^public$' }
      - has: { kind: function_modifier, regex: '^inline$' }

goodExample: internal inline fun run(block: () -> Unit) { block() }

severity: warning

  has:
    kind: modifiers
    all:

      - has: { kind: function_modifier, regex: '^suspend$' }
      - not:
          has:
            kind: annotation
            has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^JvmSynthetic$', stopBy: end }
      - not:

goodExample:

yaml:
id: no-result-getorthrow-naked
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Result.getOrThrow() rethrows the original exception with no added context and isn't wrapped in a try/catch at this call site. A naked getOrThrow() gives the caller a stack trace with no clue which operation failed. Wrap the call in a try/catch that adds context (what was being done, with which inputs) before rethrowing, or use fold { onSuccess, onFailure } / getOrElse { } to handle both branches explicitly instead."
rule:
  pattern: $OBJ.getOrThrow()
  not:
    inside:
      kind: try_expression
      stopBy: end
