yaml:
id: no-scope-function-chain
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Three or more chained scope functions (.let/.also/.apply/.run) are hard to read and debug; extract intermediate steps into named locals or a small function."
note: |
  Matches a call chain of 3+ scope functions (`.let { }.also { }.apply { }`
  and similar), detected as a `call_expression` whose receiver is itself a
  scope-function `call_expression` two levels deep. A 2-link chain
  (`.let { }.also { }`) is common and intentionally not flagged; the third
  link is where readability drops off and step-through debugging gets hard
  (a breakpoint inside the chain can't easily tell you which link's
  intermediate value you're looking at). On a 4+ link chain this rule
  reports at more than one nesting depth (once for the outermost 3-link
  window, once for the inner 3-link sub-chain it contains); that is
  expected duplicate signal for a warning-tier heuristic, not a bug.
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  all:
    - has:
        kind: call_suffix
    - has:
        kind: navigation_expression
        all:
          - has:
              kind: navigation_suffix
              has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(let|also|apply|run)$' }
          - has:
              kind: call_expression
              has:
                kind: navigation_expression
                all:
                  - has:
                      kind: navigation_suffix
                      has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(let|also|apply|run)$' }
                  - has:
                      kind: call_expression
                      has:
                        kind: navigation_expression
                        has:
                          kind: navigation_suffix
                          has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '^(let|also|apply|run)$' }
badExample: internal fun f(x: String): String = x.let { it }.also { it }.apply { }
goodExample: internal fun f(x: String): String = x.let { it }.also { it }

yaml:
id: no-singleton-object-with-state
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "A property inside an `object` singleton is mutable (`var`) or holds a mutable collection (`MutableList`/`MutableMap`/...). Every property of an `object` is process-wide shared state — mutating it is a hidden global and a data race under concurrent access. Model the state with a StateFlow/Mutex-guarded holder, or pass it explicitly instead of storing it on the singleton."
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  inside:
    kind: class_body
    inside: { kind: object_declaration }
  any:
    - has: { kind: binding_pattern_kind, regex: '^var$' }
    - has:
        kind: variable_declaration
        has:
          kind: user_type
          has:
            kind: type_identifier
            regex: '^(MutableList|MutableMap|MutableSet|MutableCollection|ArrayList|HashMap|LinkedHashMap|HashSet|LinkedHashSet)$'
note: >-
  Overlaps by design with the LAW-tier `no-var-in-object-declaration` rule (which
  blocks the `var` case with severity: error) — this style rule additionally covers
  the mutable-collection-`val` case for the same "singleton state" concern, and is
  meant to be run as a single combined check rather than a replacement for the LAW rule.

id: no-star-projection-in-public
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "KClass<*>/Class<*> in a public function's parameter or return type throws away the type information the caller could otherwise get back, and forces unchecked casts wherever the value is used. Take a reified type parameter (inline fun <reified T>) or a concrete KClass<T>/Class<T> instead of a star projection."
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  all:
    - has:
        kind: modifiers
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^public$'
    - any:
        - has:
            kind: function_value_parameters
            has:
              kind: parameter
              has:
                kind: user_type
                all:
                  - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(KClass|Class)$' }
                  - has:
                      kind: type_arguments
                      has:
                        kind: type_projection
                        not: { has: { kind: user_type } }
        - has:
            kind: user_type
            all:
              - has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(KClass|Class)$' }
              - has:
                  kind: type_arguments
                  has:
                    kind: type_projection
                    not: { has: { kind: user_type } }
              - follows: { kind: function_value_parameters, stopBy: end }
badExample: public fun register(type: KClass<*>) { }
goodExample: public fun register(type: KClass<String>) { }

yaml:
id: no-string-typed-id
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Parameter named like an id (`id`, `...Id`) is typed as raw `String`. A bare String accepts any string, so callers can pass the wrong id (or a display name) and the compiler won't catch it. Wrap it in a value class (e.g. `@JvmInline value class UserId(val value: String)`) so mismatched ids become a compile error."
rule:
  kind: parameter
  all:
    - has: { kind: simple_identifier, regex: '(^id$|Id$)' }
    - has:
        kind: user_type
        has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^String$' }
badExample: internal fun load(userId: String) { }
goodExample: internal fun load(userId: UserId) { }

yaml:
id: no-suspend-default-dispatcher
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "The entire suspend function body is `withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { ... }`; inject the dispatcher as a parameter (e.g. `context: CoroutineContext = Dispatchers.Default`) instead of hardcoding it so callers/tests can override it."
note: |
  Narrower companion to the existing `no-hardcoded-dispatcher-in-builder`
  rule, which already flags `withContext(Dispatchers.$D) { ... }` for ANY
  dispatcher, anywhere in a function body. This rule matches only the
  strongest instance of that shape: a `suspend fun`'s entire body (its `=`
  expression body, with or without a declared return type) is exactly
  `withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { ... }` — i.e. the function exists
  solely to hardcode a dispatcher hop. That specific shape is the clearest
  signal the function should just take an injected `CoroutineContext`
  parameter (defaulted to `Dispatchers.Default`) instead. A `withContext`
  call nested inside a larger block body, or using any dispatcher other
  than `Default`, is left to `no-hardcoded-dispatcher-in-builder`.
rule:
  kind: function_declaration
  any:
    - pattern: 'suspend fun $NAME($$$PARAMS): $RET = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { $$$BODY }'
    - pattern: 'suspend fun $NAME($$$PARAMS) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { $$$BODY }'
badExample: suspend fun compute(): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { 1 }
goodExample: suspend fun compute(): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { 1 }

yaml:
id: no-throws-generic-exception
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "@Throws(Exception::class) / @Throws(Throwable::class) is too broad to be useful to JVM/Swift callers that rely on it for checked-exception or NSError bridging — it documents nothing about what actually goes wrong. List the specific typed exception(s) the function can actually throw instead."
rule:
  kind: annotation
  regex: '^@Throws\(.*\b(Exception|Throwable)::class.*\)$'
badExample:
@Throws(Exception::class)
public fun f(): Int = 1
goodExample:
@Throws(IOException::class)
public fun f(): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-untyped-map-key
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "`Map<String, ...>` uses a raw String as the key. If the key set is a closed, meaningful domain (a header name, a provider id, a locale), a bare String lets any string in — typos and lookups against the wrong key compile fine and fail at runtime. Prefer a value class or enum for the key, or confirm the key genuinely is open-ended user text."
rule:
  kind: type_projection
  all:
    - has: { kind: user_type, has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^String$' } }
    - not: { follows: { kind: type_projection, stopBy: end } }
    - inside:
        kind: type_arguments
        inside:
          kind: user_type
          has: { kind: type_identifier, regex: '^(Map|MutableMap)$' }
note: >-
  Matches only the first type argument of Map/MutableMap (the key position) via
  "no preceding type_projection sibling" — Map<Foo, String> (String as the value)
  is intentionally not flagged.
badExample: internal fun f(m: Map<String, Int>): Int = 1
goodExample: internal fun f(m: Map<UserId, Int>): Int = 1

yaml:
id: no-var-in-builder
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "public var property in a *Builder class exposes a raw mutable field instead of a controlled setter API. Match the CallSettingsBuilder pattern this SDK already uses elsewhere: a private var backing field + a public fun name(value) setter method, so the builder can validate input or add fields later without it being a public-var ABI commitment (a public var also fails the no-public-mutable-var gate)."
rule:
  kind: property_declaration
  all:
    - has: { kind: binding_pattern_kind, regex: '^var$' }
    - not:
        has:
          kind: visibility_modifier
          regex: '^(private|internal|protected)$'
          stopBy: end
    - inside:
        kind: class_body
        inside:
          kind: class_declaration
          has:
            kind: type_identifier
            regex: 'Builder'

id: no-when-subject-mutation
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Reassigning the `when` subject inside a branch has no effect on branch selection (the subject is evaluated once); the mutation reads as if it changes matching but it doesn't. Use a separate local for the new value."
note: |
  Matches `when (subject) { ... }` where some branch body assigns back to
  `subject`. Uses an ast-grep shared metavariable ($SUBJECT) to require the
  when-subject identifier and the assignment target identifier be the exact
  same name, so mutating an unrelated variable inside a branch does not
  match. `when` without a subject (the boolean-branches form,
  `when { cond -> ... }`) has no `when_subject` node and never matches.
  This is purely a readability/intent trap, not a runtime bug: Kotlin
  evaluates the subject once up front, so the mutation is dead as far as
  branch dispatch is concerned — but it reads to a maintainer as if later
  branches (or a hypothetical loop) would see the new value.
rule:
  kind: when_expression
  all:
    - has:
        kind: when_subject
        has:
          kind: simple_identifier
          pattern: $SUBJECT
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: when_entry
        has:
          stopBy: end
          kind: assignment
          has:
            kind: directly_assignable_expression
            has:
              kind: simple_identifier
              pattern: $SUBJECT

id: no-part-exceeds-total-heuristic
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "A token/count PART is being compared against its TOTAL to decide the total (`if (reasoningTokens > outputTokens) ...`). A part that exceeds its total is a response violating the wire contract, not a second provider shape to infer: clamp the part into its range (`.coerceIn(0, total)`) and report the provider's total unchanged. The magnitude test cannot distinguish a malformed response from a provider reporting a text-only total, so it silently under-counts one of them."
note: |
  Found three times in this repo, all the same shape, all reporting usage that feeds cost:
  Usage.kt (UsageFromOpenAI), HuggingFaceProvider.kt (huggingFaceUsage), OpenResponsesProvider.kt
  (openResponsesUsage). Each sat two lines below a CORRECT clamp of the same kind
  (`cachedTokens.coerceIn(0, promptTokens)`), so the asymmetry was visible in-function and still
  copied forward twice.

  `OutputTokenBreakdown` rejects parts exceeding total at construction, so in a SHARED parser the
  branch exists to dodge a constructor guard that is telling the truth. The right response there is
  to clamp, not to widen the total until it fits.

  ONE legitimate shape, which is why this is a warning and not a law: a provider that genuinely
  reports a text-only total gets a NAMED, provider-specific correction — `fixDeepInfraUsage` in
  DeepInfraFacade.kt is the repo's example, and DeepInfra is exactly the "second provider shape" a
  magnitude test in a shared parser cannot identify. The invariant is therefore: shared parsers
  CLAMP; a provider quirk gets a named function in that provider's facade. If this fires on a
  shared parser, clamp it. If it fires on a named provider correction, that is the sanctioned form.

  Note that even the sanctioned form inherits the magnitude test's blind spot — a text-only provider
  whose reasoning is SHORTER than its completion still passes through uncorrected. Detecting the
  provider by identity rather than by magnitude would close that; it needs provider knowledge to
  confirm, so it is a question for a maintainer, not a mechanical fix.
rule:
  kind: if_expression
  all:
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: comparison_expression
        all:
          - has:
              stopBy: end
              kind: simple_identifier
              regex: '(?i)(reasoning|cached|cache|text)\w*[Tt]okens?$'
          - has:
              stopBy: end
              kind: simple_identifier
              regex: '(?i)^(output|completion|prompt|input|total)\w*[Tt]okens?$'
    # Only the shape that DECIDES a total from the comparison — an assert/require/clamp using the
    # same two identifiers is the correct handling and must not be flagged.
    - not:
        has:
          stopBy: end
          kind: simple_identifier
          regex: '^(require|check|coerceIn|coerceAtMost|error)$'
    # The sanctioned form is exempt STRUCTURALLY, not by prose in the note: a named provider-specific
    # correction (`fixDeepInfraUsage`) for a provider that really does report a text-only total. With
    # all four shared-parser instances fixed, leaving it unexempt made the rule's entire live output
    # the one site its own note calls correct — a 0:1 signal ratio, which is the "fires on the
    # sanctioned pattern" failure this pack has already been burned by three times.
    - not:
        inside:
          stopBy: end
          kind: function_declaration
          has:
            kind: simple_identifier
            regex: '^fix[A-Z]'

fun f(requestHeaders: Map<String, String>): Map<String, String> =

yaml:
id: no-credential-denylist-filter
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "Header map filtered by EXCLUSION (`!in blocked` / `!key.equals(\"Authorization\")`). Naming the headers to remove only covers the names you thought of — a `Cookie`, a `Proxy-Authorization`, a host's bespoke `x-org-token` all survive. Filter by INCLUSION instead: keep the names you can name, drop everything else."
note: |
  Historical bug (review 4791043656 and the four passes after it): the Fireworks image download
  filtered caller headers with a two-name denylist — `Authorization` and `x-api-key`, the two the SDK
  sets itself — while `requestHeaders` also carried whatever the host configured through
  `settings.headers` / `params.headers`. The destination came from the provider's own
  `result.sample`, so a `Cookie` went to a third-party CDN. The FIRST fix was another denylist, of
  three names, and an injected `X-Org-Token` walked through it. The shape failed twice before an
  allowlist replaced it.

  The one live hit, GoogleVertexProvider.googleVertexAnthropicHeaders, has now been reviewed and is
  CORRECT — recorded here so the next reader does not re-litigate it, and so this rule is not left
  as a permanent warning that points at nothing. It strips the Anthropic-protocol headers
  (anthropic-version/-beta, x-api-key, Authorization, User-Agent) from a header set that is then
  sent to VERTEX, the endpoint the caller explicitly chose by constructing this provider. A caller's
  own `Cookie` reaching the provider the caller is calling is not a disclosure; the Fireworks bug was
  a disclosure because the destination came out of a provider response and was a third-party CDN. So
  the namespace is closed in the only sense that matters, and an inclusion filter is not even
  expressible here: the intent is "forward whatever the caller set, minus the wire keys Vertex
  rejects", which no allowlist can enumerate.

  It is left FIRING rather than exempted because ast-grep can only ignore by file glob, and a
  file-wide ignore would bless every future denylist filter added to GoogleVertexProvider.kt — the
  same path-keyed blindness that had to be fixed in detect-provider-asset-credential-leak.py. With
  the style-rule count ratcheted at 1, a SECOND such filter anywhere in the tree fails the gate,
  which is the coverage this rule is actually for.

  Warning, not law: an exclusion filter over a CLOSED namespace (dropping two known wire keys from a
  JSON object you built) is fine. It is only dangerous over an open one, and "open" is a judgement
  the pattern cannot make. Paired with detect-provider-asset-credential-leak.py, which owns the
  blocking check for the specific case where the destination is provider-supplied.
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  all:
    # Only HEADER maps. An exclusion filter over a closed namespace — dropping two known keys from a
    # JSON object you built — is fine, and scoping to headers is what keeps this from firing on the
    # 18 legitimate filterKeys/filterNot sites in this tree and training dismissal.
    - has:
        kind: navigation_expression
        has:
          kind: simple_identifier
          regex: '(?i)headers$'
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: simple_identifier
        regex: '^filterKeys$'
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: lambda_literal
        has:
          stopBy: end
          any:
            # `key !in blocked`
            - kind: check_expression
            # `!key.equals("Authorization", ...)`
            - kind: prefix_expression
              has:
                kind: call_expression
                stopBy: end

id: no-ignored-claim-result
language: kotlin
severity: warning
message: "The Boolean result of a CLAIM-style call is discarded. These functions return false to say the state changed under you — a concurrent close won, the CAS lost, the buffer refused the value — so dropping the result silently takes the success path on the losing branch. Bind it and handle false."
note: |
  Historical bug (review 4813532855 + the audit that followed): `Experimental_StdioMCPTransport.start`
  called `lifecycle.setReader(readerJob)` as a bare statement. setReader no-ops when the lifecycle is
  no longer Active, so a `close()` that won the transition left the freshly spawned child process and
  its FDs leaked, `process` non-null, and the transport permanently Closed while `send()` could still
  write to the orphan. The fix made setReader return Boolean — and then the FIRST version of that fix
  had its own defect, because "not Active" is Closed OR Idle-after-reader-exit and only Closed means
  the caller still owns the child.

  Both halves of that came from the same root: a state transition that can LOSE, reported through a
  value nobody had to read. `compareAndSet` and `tryEmit` are the same shape from the stdlib —
  a dropped `tryEmit` silently discards an event on a full buffer.

  Scoped to a curated vocabulary rather than "any Boolean-returning call", because the useful
  invariant is about claim/transition APIs, not about every ignored return.
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  all:
    # A bare statement: the parent is the statement list, so nothing consumes the value.
    - inside:
        kind: statements
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: simple_identifier
        regex: '^(compareAndSet|weakCompareAndSet|setReader|tryEmit|tryLock|tryAcquire|tryClaim|claim|offer)$'

id: no-uncapped-response-body
language: kotlin
severity: error
message: "Raw `bodyAsBytes()`/`bodyAsText()`/`body<ByteArray>()`/`readBytes()` reads a response with no size limit. Use `with(HttpTransport) { response.bodyAsBytesCapped(url) }` / `bodyAsTextCapped(url)` for a content cap, or `HttpTransport.downloadCapped(client, url)` when the bytes come from a host you do not control — only that one bounds MEMORY, because Ktor pre-buffers every `client.request(...)` body."
note: |
  This is the hardened-helper-beside-unhardened-primitive shape. HttpTransport.bodyAsTextCapped /
  bodyAsBytesCapped were written precisely because an unbounded body read is a memory-exhaustion
  vector on a KMP client with no server-side sandbox — and then 14 call sites went on calling the
  raw Ktor primitive anyway, including a download of a CALLER-supplied URL
  (OpenAICompatibleModels.openAICompatibleImageFileBytes) and every audio/image byte path. Writing
  the safe helper does not remove the unsafe one from scope, so nothing made the unmigrated sites
  visible: MCP, McpOAuth, Fal, Luma and Replicate used the capped form while Deepgram, Hume,
  ElevenLabs, LMNT, Prodia, Bedrock, xAI, HuggingFace, OpenResponses and the OpenAI-compatible
  transports did not, and the split was invisible in review.

  Deliberately targets the CALL, not the import, so `with(HttpTransport) { bodyAsBytesCapped(url) }`
  and the extension-receiver form (`bodyAsBytes()` with no explicit receiver, inside an
  `HttpResponse.` extension) are both covered — the receiver-less form is how four of the sites
  were written, so an import- or navigation-shaped rule would have missed them.

  Streaming paths are unaffected: they use `bodyAsChannel()`, which never buffers, and this rule
  does not mention it. If a genuinely unbounded read is ever needed, pass an explicit large
  `maxBytes` to the capped helper — the cap becomes a reviewed number rather than an absence.

  The first version required an EMPTY argument list (`not: has: value_argument`), on the reasoning
  that `bodyAsBytes()` never takes one. That clause bought nothing and cost the whole wall:
  `bodyAsText` DOES take an optional `fallbackCharset`, so `response.bodyAsText(Charsets.UTF_8)` —
  a natural thing to write on a charset-sensitive provider — walked straight through a green gate.
  Arity is not the invariant; the function being called is. The alias forms go in for the same
  reason: `bodyAsBytes()` IS `body<ByteArray>()`, so anyone writing the underlying form bypassed a
  rule that named only the sugar.
rule:
  kind: call_expression
  any:
    - has:
        stopBy: end
        kind: simple_identifier
        regex: '^(bodyAsBytes|bodyAsText|readBytes)$'
    # `body<ByteArray>()` / `body<String>()` — the underlying form the two above are sugar for.
    # Scoped by TYPE ARGUMENT so the many legitimate `body<SomeWireDto>()` deserializations, whose
    # size is bounded by the parse, are not swept in.
    - all:
        - has:
            stopBy: end
            kind: simple_identifier
            regex: '^body$'
        - has:
            kind: call_suffix
            has:
              kind: type_arguments
              has:
                stopBy: end
                kind: type_identifier
                regex: '^(ByteArray|String)$'
badExample: suspend fun readIt(response: HttpResponse): ByteArray = response.bodyAsBytes()
goodExample:
suspend fun readIt(response: HttpResponse, url: String): ByteArray =
    with(HttpTransport) { response.bodyAsBytesCapped(url) }
